newsitem.title: USA: Saudis see recent oil price drop as short-lived.
newsitem.headline: Saudis see recent oil price drop as short-lived.

text.p: Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer, expects the recent decline in world oil prices to end once U.S. refineries come out of maintenance and the market starts to look toward spring gasoline demand, according to Gulf sources.
"It's normal that it (the market) goes down in February and early March," said one source.

World oil prices are at six-month lows. Benchmark Brent crude has fallen by more than $5 over the last six weeks to less than $20 per barrel. But Gulf sources said they still expected Brent to average $20-$25 per barrel in 1997.

"What's expected in the next couple of weeks is the market will start to refocus on the gasoline stock levels and consumption and refineries will end their maintenance ... which will increase the demand for crude," said one source.
Officials said prices would also be boosted by lower oil production from the North Sea where some fields are scheduled to undergo maintenance in the spring.
"You are going to go into the second quarter with greater refinery runs than we have now, low gasoline stock levels, higher gasoline consumption and lower crude production," the source said.

Gasoline stocks in the United States for the week ending February 14 stood at 206 million barrels, while refinery runs were at 13.4 million barrels per day, according to American Petroleum Institute statistics.
"If you combine all these factors, we feel that the price will rebound," one source said.
A crude-buying spree from India or China could also bolster prices, but their demand is less predictable. Countries like China and India tend to withdraw from the market when prices are high.
"When the price is going down, as it is now, they will go to the market and buy," one source said. "We really don't know this time what impact it will have."
